https://www.breitbart.com/europe/2026/08.text: Advanced sea drones provided by a tech company, also contracted to the United States Military, contained Chinese components sending data from Britain back to Beijing, a whistleblower report claims. The UK Ministry of Defence was forced to issue denials after claims emerged that the country’s new generation of sea drones (‘uncrewed surface vessels’) contained cameras built with Chinese components which were sending data home without the knowledge of the military or the company that built them. Conservative-leaning broadsheet The Daily Telegraph cited the remarks of a source within the military who blew the whistle on Chinese components built into scout drones communicating with an Internet Protocol (IP) address inside China, who said: “This is major failure to check origins of components and we have lost confidence in the platform”. Per the report, the components were installed inside a camera system fitted to K3 Scout drones, which the Navy says can be used for “surveillance, force protection and precision strikes”. Acquired by the Royal Navy as part of a £12 million contract as the British military experiments with emerging drone technologies, the K3 is built by UK-based Kraken Technology, which has also boasted of a $49 million agreement with the United States Special Operations Command. Respected defence blog Navy Lookout notes that the K3 is fitted with a ‘Night Navigator 3000 series’ Electro-Optical/Infra-Red camera system, which is mounted prominently on the top of the drone boat’s superstructure to give remote operators a clear view around the craft. That gimballed camera assembly is made by Canadian tech company Current Scientific Corporation, but it isn’t clear that this is definitely the system impacted by Chinese components, as the craft may have more than one camera fitted. Former Royal Navy Admiral and Falklands War veteran known for sinking an Argentinian submarine in 1982, Chris Parry, reflected on the revelations and said that, in his view, accidentally allowing internet-connected Chinese components into a Royal Navy boat should mean a “major fine” for the supplier and a ban from competing for future contracts. According to the Royal Navy’s own account, drone technology is a major part of the government’s vision for the future of defence. Recent statements by the Navy note that “uncrewed systems are no longer a future concept for the Royal Navy and Royal Marines; they have been delivering operational effect for the past four years and are in service today”, and that the Kraken K3 has already “undergone thorough testing in UK waters”. Earlier this year, the Navy trialled dropping the K3 out of the back of an aircraft to test rapid deployment of the craft in foreign waters. The Ministry of Defence moved fast to control the story and issued a statement that didn’t deny their new scout drone had been transmitting data to China, but did insist that nothing of importance had been sent to Beijing. The department said: The first duty of government is national security, and we take the security of our equipment, networks and data extremely seriously. A routine cyber-vulnerability assessment identified an issue affecting a Kraken Unmanned Surface Vessel sub-system used by the Royal Navy. A thorough investigation found no evidence of MoD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally. Our assurance and testing processes are designed to identify and address potential vulnerabilities early, and we continue to undertake routine security activity across our systems and equipment. Boat builder Kraken also commented and said through a spokesman: We are aware that some third-party, NDAA-compliant cameras had a small number of components originating from outside the UK. After a full audit by both Kraken and the Royal Navy we are confident no sensitive information has ever been shared outside of intended channels and any potential vulnerabilities have been identified and closed. Despite the minimising statements, The Daily Telegraph reports that the issue was considered serious enough for the uncrewed drone boats to be isolated from the internet, and that concerns were raised about whether sensitive military discussions may have been held in proximity to the compromised craft. The vulnerabilities of technology to Chinese components potentially inserting backdoors for foreign intelligence into equipment are well understood in the United Kingdom, yet it appears that, in the case of these seagoing scout drones, they were accepted into service earlier this year without a full understanding of what was inside. The consequences of such decisions are clear: the Huawei debacle of 2020 saw the then-British government of Boris Johnson having to back out of a contract with Chinese tech firm Huawei to build a part of the nation’s incoming 5G telecoms network. The government had been keen to stay with the Chinese state-controlled business as the best value-for-money bid for the project, even in the face of security warnings about allowing China to take hold of the UK’s internet backbone, pushing ahead even in the face of a rebellion by its own lawmakers . Those most responsible for security seem sensible to the risk, however. Both Britain and Poland’s militaries have banned Chinese electric vehicles from sensitive military sites — given that modern electric cars are covered in sensors, cameras, and microphones, and have internet connectivity — and the U.S. military has blocked Chinese EV companies from bidding on contracts given their close ties to the Chinese government. Composite: supplied Egypt UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’ Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Thu 27 Aug 2026 04.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism. Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel. Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”. The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid. The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt. Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers. “There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect. Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos. But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.” Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted. Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials. The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply. Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government. On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years. Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad. Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction. The Foreign Office has been approached for comment. Speaking on television, Francken warned Baltic nations against cornering Belgium over the issue, given the assets are largely held at the Belgian clearinghouse Euroclear. by Euractiv | Aug. 30, 2026, 2:52 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Belgium’s Minister of Defence and Foreign Trade Theo Francken speaks during the presentation ceremony of the H145M Light Utility Helicopter at the Beauvechain Air Base in Beauvechain on June 23, 2026. (Photo by JONAS ROOSENS / Belga / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Belgium is standing firm against using frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine, as four EU countries push to resurrect the scheme. “This is non-negotiable, the door is closed,” Theo Francken, the defence minister, told Terzaken, on Flemish TV channel VRT, on Friday night. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . This week Sweden, Poland, the Netherlands and Spain called upon the European Commission to explore new ways to harness around €200 billion in immobilised Russian assets to support Ukraine. At a dramatic European summit last December, Bart De Wever, the Belgian leader, shot down an effort led by Germany and the European Commission, to fashion a €210 billion ($243 billion) ‘reparations loan’ for Ukraine, arguing it would leave the Benelux nation exposed to Russian legal retribution. Advertisement Most of the assets are held at Euroclear in Belgium. “Our prime minister will stand firm,” Francken added. Noting that Belgium’s resistance has generated resentment, he singled out the Baltic states – who are the strongest supporters of the reparations loan – for refusing to drop it. “They should also be careful about constantly bringing this issue up again and putting us in a corner. I don’t think that is wise,” Francken said, pointing at the Baltics. Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia receive a lot of support from Belgium, he pointed out. Other Topics of Interest Russian Strikes Hit Odesa Food Hub, Kill 1 in Zaporizhzhia Drone Attack Russian drone and bomb strikes across Ukraine have killed one woman in Zaporizhzhia, injured ten others, and destroyed a food warehouse in Odesa. Francken’s tough tone differs somewhat from the way Maxime Prévot, the Belgian foreign minister, has talked about the scheme this month. Prévot appeared to leave the door open to using the immobilised assets, this month, on the condition that all legal responsibility is fairly shared out among EU countries. The Swedish letter acknowledged the legal risks inherent in using the Russian assets, and stated that no country should bear a disproportionate burden. European foreign ministers will discuss the topic at an meeting in Ireland next week. Magyar Péter bejegyzésére nem felháborodásból írt, hanem korrigálni akarta a miniszterelnököt. „Egyszerűen azt éreztem, hogy tudom, hogy mennyi nő dolgozott ezen, és korrigálni szerettem volna, és odaírtam, hogy igen, a nők is ott voltak, és fontos szerepet töltöttek be. Nem biztos, hogy még egyszer ilyet írnék, azért mert félreérthető volt. Az a rövidke mivolta annak a közlésnek olyan szúrósnak tűnt, miközben tényleg az volt bennem, hogy én nagyon becsülöm a kolléganőimet, Orbán Anitát, Lannert Juditot, Lőrincz Viktóriát, akik miniszterként helytállnak” – mondta az esetről Forsthoffer. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-summi.text: EU leaders locked horns over everything from climate rules to migration policy and Ukraine’s long-term financial needs during two days of tense discussions in Brussels. But despite calls for urgent action, the main takeaway from Thursday and Friday’s European Council summit is that key decisions have been delayed to a later date. With elections looming in Spain and France, and as leaders’ positions seem more entrenched than ever, nothing of substance was put down in ink. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who made the trip to Belgium, did not receive much more than warm embraces and kind words. Advertisement Advertisement Speaking to journalists during a packed news conference, Ukraine’s wartime leader urged his European counterparts to come up with a financial plan or risk facing an unprecedented migration crisis with “20 million Ukrainians” fleeing to Europe. “The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience,” Zelenskyy said. “This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.” But two diplomats told POLITICO that capitals would continue exploring a range of options to meet Kyiv’s needs, including a potential further loan from the EU. A debate over whether to mobilize some €300 billion in Russian frozen assets to help Ukraine is a case in point. Nearly a year after EU leaders rejected using the assets amid objections from Belgium, France and Italy, several countries have asked for the option to be revisited, and top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas had said frozen assets would be on the table when leaders met in Brussels. But after hours of talks about Ukraine, “nothing has changed,” said Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. “The money is not lost but in my belief nothing has happened since we had the discussion last time.” “In the short term, money to support Ukraine must come from other sources than the frozen assets,” he concluded. Advertisement Advertisement Two EU diplomats told POLITICO that the European Commission and EU capitals were working on other financing options, including seeking funds from Ukraine’s non-EU allies, mobilizing as yet untapped EU funds and drawing up another joint EU loan to complement the €90 billion loan they agreed on last year. The leaders “didn’t spend a lot of time” trying to come up with a plan to fund Ukraine in 2027, after Zelenskyy said his country would face a €70 billion budget hole next year, European Council President António Costa said. “We agreed immediately that we need to address the additional needs of financing Ukraine in 2027 and asked Commission to come up with concrete proposal.” Yet leaders declined to endorse any of those options during news conferences at the end of the summit. Money talks drag on The gathering had also been billed as a chance for leaders to break a months-old deadlock over the size and shape of the EU’s nearly €2 trillion long-term budget. French President Emmanuel Macron, who leaves office next year ahead of a presidential election in April and June, warned leaders that he would no longer have a political mandate to ink a deal if no deal was concluded by the end of this year. But despite hours of talks on Thursday, neither the frugal camp led by Germany — which advocates a smaller budget — nor the “Friends of Cohesion” group calling for a larger envelope had made any substantial step toward each other. Advertisement Advertisement “I think [a decision] is possible by the end of the year,” Macron told journalists at the summit’s conclusion, adding that failure to strike a deal this year would not “be a good method from a democratic standpoint.” Instead, leaders spent much of the two-day summit trying to gain a tactical upper hand over rivals on EU climate rules and migration policy. Trench warfare A push led Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to water down an emissions trading scheme known as ETS2 hijacked discussions for hours on Thursday. But despite wider support for Tusk’s position than at previous summits, it was easily defeated by countries that support the current scheme. On migration, Denmark, Italy and Poland led a determined effort to harden the EU’s position, proposing tweaks to the summit’s conclusions that would have explicitly linked irregular migration to crime rates and branded the phenomenon a threat to the cohesion of European societies. The proposal, which ultimately won support from a group of around 10 countries including Hungary, according to two EU diplomats, also indirectly took aim at Spain, where Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s decision to regularize some 1 million irregular migrants has sparked clashes with Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen. Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that the Commission would put forward an emergency response framework before the end of the year to allow EU countries to respond to a sudden mass movement, such as the one that caused chaos in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta over the summer. Advertisement Advertisement But the effort led by Meloni and Frederiksen ended in defeat, with the proposed paragraphs deleted from the summit’s final conclusions, which only contained a truncated version. Macron criticized the discussions on migration, saying they had been excessively “politicized.” “It was a bad debate because it has been highly politicized and it has been a major source of division around the table,” the French president said.

https://www.newscentralasia.net/2026/10/.text: Home » A Salute to Germany: Unity Built on Resolve Tariq Saeedi Germany marked its Day of Unity on 3 October, the 36th anniversary of reunification. It remains one of the most remarkable political achievements of the modern era. Two states, divided by a fortified frontier and opposed ideologies, were peacefully joined into one nation, something many contemporary observers thought impossible. It is worth setting aside the political rhetoric and saluting Germany and its people for it. The credit begins in the East. In 1989, ordinary East Germans, marching in Leipzig and in cities across the country, brought down a regime without bloodshed. International conditions mattered too: Hungary’s opening of its border, Soviet restraint under Mikhail Gorbachev, and the Two Plus Four Treaty that settled the question with the wartime Allies. But the courage that set the process in motion belonged to the people of the German Democratic Republic. What followed was an extraordinary national effort. The Federal Republic, with one of the world’s strongest economies, committed enormous financial and administrative resources to the East. Roads and railways were rebuilt, a dated telecommunications network was replaced, and the social safety net was extended. The task rested on institutional strengths long associated with Germany: precision, long-term planning, administrative discipline and a strong work ethic, qualities of civic culture rather than anything inborn. The achievement was not free of cost, and honest tribute acknowledges this. A simple rule of geopolitics holds: the longer a division lasts, the harder it is to heal. Over four decades, two economic systems, two political cultures and two ways of thinking about everyday life hardened on either side of the frontier. Bridging them meant the closure of state enterprises, sudden industrial dislocation, high unemployment in the East, and a generational effort to reconcile different experiences and expectations. Some of those invisible walls take longer to dismantle than concrete ones. Differences in income, wealth and economic opportunity between East and West persist today, and many Germans still feel them. That Germany absorbed these shocks without losing its democratic stability or social cohesion speaks to the resilience of its citizens. There were hard years, and at the turn of the century Germany was widely regarded as Europe’s economic laggard. Yet the country adjusted, reformed and recovered, and it emerged as the anchor of the European Union. Today a unified Germany shows that deep political, economic and psychological divides can be bridged when a society has the will and the patience to do so. It is also a reminder that unity is not an event but a continuing task.
